Objects, Verbs, Census






TipBreaking Down R Code





result <- filter(counties, population > 50000) # keep the big ones!




result - this is an object
<- - this can also be =, it is an assignment arrow
filter - this is a function
counties - this is input data
population > 50000 - this is an argument







TipPackages





Packages are things that can be installed and called upon when you are running your code




install.packages("dplyr") - this only needs to be done once
library(dplyr) - this is like a book. You need to run this every time you use r

Verbs

filter() - picks Rows
select() - picks Columns
mutate() - adds a new Computed Column
arrange() - change order of rows in ascending or descending order
group_by() + summarize() - many rows become few. For example, for a dataframe with many states and income levels, it can group it by state and it can summarize the income levels.



Manipulating the Data (Example - Novice)






TipStep 1





filler(counties, moe_pct >10)









TipStep 2





arrange(Step1, desc(moe_pct))









TipStep 3





Select(Step2,NAME, (moe_pct)




However, this is a very novice way of doing things because it creates more unnecessary data frames that pollute your workspace



Thinking of Advanced Ways






Tip





While it is good to think about the step-by-step process to be clear about how you are manipulating the data, you can start using the % code to string together functions to compute your data output without creating the files in between.




For Example
New__Data <- Counties %>% 
  filter(moe_pct > 10) %>% 
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  Select(NAME, moepct)






Warning



Take note that everything is case sensitive in R. A good rule of thumb is to put everything in lowercase.





The Census






TipThe Census





The census is a great source of data that we will use. It is mandated by the constitution to count the number of people that live there on an interval of every 10 years (Decennial Census, created by James Madison). Every person that is in the US (legally or illegally) is asked 10 questions on a 10 year basis.









TipAmerican Community Survey (ACS)





Created in 2005. It replaced the long form of the Decennial Census. It has more data that we are interested in (things like income, travel patterns). Roughly 3% of households are surveyed. From the sample, an estimate for the population is derived. There are two versions of the ACS.




The 1-year ACS: Only for places with >65,000 people (metropolitan level). While it is the most current, we don’t often use it in our analysis because we don’t often get the neighborhood level.
The 3-year ACS (now deprecated): not in use
The 5-year ACS: Goes down to block group, census tract…etc. This means that when you get ACS data for the year 2016 (for example), you are accessing the 5-year average of the neighborhood.


tidycensus






Tiptidycensus



tidycensus is where you can access the census through r in a simple way



It is formatted as such: B19013_001E


B is the base table
191032 is the table number
001E is the line number
E is the estimate of the MOE



Census Tracts

They are organised from State > County > Tract

A tract is a ‘neighborhood’ or around 5-8,000 people. However, the boundaries keep changing. This is why there are longtitudinal tracts like NHGIS (University of Minnesota) or LTDB (Brown University) that help combat this issue.






Warning



There are also things called block groups, but they are very unreliable. They are not representative, and you should not use this.




GEOID






Tip



It used to be an identifier. This is how you decode it.



Sample GEOID

4210100001001


42 - State
101 - County
000100 - Tract
1 - Block Group







Tip



These numbers are stored in strings. You need to keep the GEOID as a string to keep the 0s at the beginning of the first nine GEOIDS (for states that begin with A)








Warning



90% of joining issues are because of type errors between strings and numbers for the GEOID that will result in a failed join.

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim
text:
The Question
In 2018, WHYY published an article New Census figures on Philly neighborhoods show inequality, high numbers of whites living in poverty, stating many claims about the changes to the state of poverty and inequality in the city. While the claims in the article are supported with data from the ACS5, the author only briefly mentions the margins of error embedded within the data that has the potential to undermine their findings. In this report, I will dive into the margins of error between the two data sets to determine if the conclusions drawn within the article are statistically significant.

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim
text:
Part 1: Reconstructing the Data
We begin first with sourcing the ACS data through tidycensus.

Variables
The variables selected in the reconstruction of their analysis are:







Variable
ACS5 Code




Median Household Income in the past 12 months
B19013_001


Poverty Status (Income in the past 12 months below poverty level)
B17001_002


Summary of Poverty Status Population
B17001_001





ACS Selection
The ACS5 was selected for this project to be in line with the analysis from the article. Similarly, the two periods selected were 2006-2010 and 2013-2017. As the ACS5 data is aggregated across a period of 5 years, the singular selection of ACS5 2010 and ACS5 2017 maps onto the time periods stated above.


Assumptions
The assumptions of this project are that the census boundaries and methods did not change between the two time periods chosen. It was also assumed that the census tract boundaries and the neighborhoods used for comparison were comparable. This assumption had to be made because the article’s scope of analysis utilized unofficial neighborhood maps due to their easily identifiable nature by Philadelphia residents.
It was noted that the two periods in the article (2006-2010 and 2013-2017) do not overlap. This is crucial to ensure that the data being compared is not counted twice within the analysis.

For each census tract in both periods, the poverty rate was computed as the share of the tract population falling below the federal poverty line. The margin of error for this rate was derived using moe_prop().
When opening the data, it is observed that certain census tracts return a NaN value for the chosen variables. When matched with the census tract shapefiles and the map of Philadelphia, most of these tracts are aligned with the Airports (Philadelphia International Airport and the Northeast Philadelphia Airport) and parks that do not have high residential populations, thus resulting in a lack of data. These were left in the dataset to ensure the geometry of the Philadelphia area remained recognizable to the general public.


Calculating the Coefficient of Variation and the Reliability


Show code
# CV and reliability

phl_data_2010 <- phl_data_2010 %>%
  mutate(
    cv = (poverty_moe_pct / 1.645) / poverty_pct * 100,
    reliability = case_when(
      cv < 12  ~ "Reliable",
      cv <= 40 ~ "Somewhat Reliable",
      TRUE     ~ "Unreliable"
    )
  )

phl_data_2017 <- phl_data_2017 %>%
  mutate(
    cv = (poverty_moe_pct / 1.645) / poverty_pct * 100,
    reliability = case_when(
      cv < 12  ~ "Reliable",
      cv <= 40 ~ "Somewhat Reliable",
      TRUE     ~ "Unreliable"
    )
  )


To assess how much weight can be placed on each tract’s estimate, a coefficient of variation (CV) was computed by converting the MOE back to a standard error and expressing it as a percentage of the estimate. Tracts were then flagged into three reliability tiers following Jurjevich et al. (2018): CVs below 12% are considered reliable, between 12% and 40% somewhat reliable, and above 40% unreliable.
The tables below summarize tract-level reliability for both periods. A large share of tracts fall into the somewhat reliable or unreliable categories, particularly in low-population areas, which is a known limitation of ACS5 data due to sampling limitations and varied populations across census tracts.

For 2006-2010


Show code
# Creating the reliability tables

library(gt)

reliability_table_2010 <- phl_data_2010 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  mutate(
    dot = case_when(
      cv < 12  ~ "🟢",
      cv <= 40 ~ "🟡",
      TRUE     ~ "🔴"
    ),
    flag = case_when(
      cv < 12  ~ "Reliable",
      cv <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE     ~ "Unreliable"
    ),
    NAME = str_remove(NAME, ", Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania")
  ) %>%
  arrange(flag) %>%
  select(dot, NAME, poverty_pct, poverty_moe_pct, cv, flag) 
  

reliability_table_2010 %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(columns = c(poverty_pct, poverty_moe_pct), decimals = 0) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = cv, decimals = 1) %>%
  cols_label(
    dot      = "",
    NAME     = "County",
    poverty_pct = "Estimate of Poverty Percent",
    poverty_moe_pct      = "MOE",
    cv       = "CV (%)",
    flag     = "Reliability"
  ) %>%
  cols_align(align = "center", columns = dot) %>%

Reliability thresholds follow Jurjevich et al. (2018): CV < 12% reliable, 12–40% somewhat reliable, > 40% unreliable.











Testing the Results for Statistical Significance
To test whether observed changes between the two periods are statistically meaningful, the two datasets were combined into a single wide-format table with one row per tract. The change in poverty rate between 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 was then computed alongside its margin of error. Following the ACS convention that published MOEs reflect 90% confidence intervals, each MOE was first converted to a standard error by dividing by 1.645 (the z-estimate for a 90% confidence interval). The standard error of the difference was derived by taking the square root of the sum of squared standard errors from each period (the standard formula for the uncertainty of a difference between two independent estimates). A z-score was then calculated by dividing the change by its standard error. A tract’s change is considered statistically distinguishable from zero at 90% confidence when the absolute z-score exceeds 1.645. The same procedure was applied to median household income as well.


Show code
# Binding results

poverty_wide <- bind_rows(
  phl_data_2010 %>%
    st_drop_geometry() %>%
    select(GEOID, NAME, poverty_pct, poverty_moe_pct) %>%
    mutate(period = "2006-2010"),
  phl_data_2017 %>%
    st_drop_geometry() %>%
    select(GEOID, NAME, poverty_pct, poverty_moe_pct) %>%
    mutate(period = "2013-2017")
) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from  = period,
    values_from = c(poverty_pct, poverty_moe_pct)
  )


# testing results

results_poverty <- poverty_wide %>%
  mutate(
    change      = `poverty_pct_2013-2017` - `poverty_pct_2006-2010`,
    se_1        = `poverty_moe_pct_2006-2010` / 1.645,
    se_2        = `poverty_moe_pct_2013-2017` / 1.645,
    se_diff     = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2),
    moe_diff    = se_diff * 1.645,
    z           = change / se_diff,
    significant = abs(z) > 1.645
  )

results_poverty %>%
  count(significant)

2 TRUE           63
3 NA              8

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim
text:
Part 3: Adjudicate

The Article’s Claims
The article makes many claims regarding the changes to Philadelphia’s poverty rate, white poverty, and income levels. The section below sorts out the different claims by three distinctions: 1) Supported by the Data, 2) Not Supported by the data, and 3) Cannot be Determined

1) Supported by the Data
The article makes a claim that Fairhill is the neighborhood with the highest inequality based on percentage in poverty (61%) based on the ACS5 2017 data. Drawing from our own analysis of the data through the census tracts, the average poverty rate of the three census tracts that best fit the Fairhill neighborhood boundary is 61.5%, thus demonstrating that the claims in the article regarding the high inequality in Fairhill are supported by the data.


Show code
fairhill <- phl_data_2017 %>%
  filter(GEOID %in% c("42101017500", "42101017601", "42101017602"))

mean_fairhill <-
  mean(fairhill$poverty_pct)

print(mean_fairhill)


[1] 61.50695




2) Not Supported by the Data
The article goes in depth into the rise of poverty in the neighborhood of Eastwick. From their data, the authors claim that there was a rise of 14 percentage points in the poverty rate in Eastwick: Rising from a 12% poverty rate in 2010 to a 26% poverty rate in 2017. When comparing to the ACS data at the census tract level used in this project, it is observed that the average of the four census tracts the most closely aligns with the neighborhood of Eastwick results in a 17% increase in the percentage of poverty that is higher than the reported figures in the article.


Show code
eastwick <- results_poverty %>%
  filter(GEOID %in% c("42101005400", "42101005600", "42101005500", "42101006000" ))

mean_eastwick <- 
  mean(eastwick$change)

print(mean_eastwick)


[1] 17.0232




3) Cannot be Determined
The claims stated by the article regarding white poverty cannot be determined as there is no race-disaggregated data relating to the poverty rate. Some of the article’s other claims relating to specific neighborhoods that do not line up with census tract boundaries also cannot be determined.

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim
text:
Part 4: Rewrite
New census data confirms that poverty in Philadelphia remains deeply concentrated, with tracts in the Fairhill area of North Philadelphia showing poverty rates averaging around 61 percent. This is among the highest in the city. However, the picture is more uncertain than the headline figures in the article suggest. Of Philadelphia’s 384 census tracts, only 63 show a change in poverty rate between 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 that is statistically distinguishable from zero at 90% confidence. For the remaining 313 tracts, the margins of error in the underlying survey data are wide enough that the apparent changes in poverty rate cannot be reliably separated from sampling noise. Thus, claims about dramatic poverty increases in specific neighborhoods, and about surging white poverty across the Northeast, rest on point estimates that the data cannot confidently support at the tract level.

text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.
In this analysis, I look at Median Home Value across counties in Illinois, and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably.

The average population of counties with high confidence was 240,766.12, while the average population of counties with low confidence was 7350.818. Counties with moderate levels of confidence had an average population of 19,387. The pattern is generally that with higher populations, the level of confidence in the data increases.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy

We know the least about the 11 counties with the lowest confidence levels. This would be Pope County, Bond County, Scott County, Massac County, Pulaski County, Calhoun County, Brown County, Hamilton County, Jasper County, Alexander County, and Hardin County, which had a margin of error percent range of 10.275 to 34.099. As seen in the above table, these counties also have lower average populations compared to the rest of the state.
As the ACS5 already measures a slice of the county population, smaller counties like Hardin County (with about a population of 3623) will have smaller samples that lead to higher variability in the median. With a small population, the statistical standard error increases, resulting in imprecision within the data. Hence, we can conclude that the states with the lower populations are the communities that we know the least about from the ACS5 data.
If a state agency allocates funding using the variable of median home values, there is a high probability that the ACS5 estimate of the true median of a county may be higher than the actual value. This error in the estimate may result in low confidence counties appearing wealthier than they actually are and receiving less aid than they would need, thus resulting in an inequitable provision of welfare funding.

Tip



Take note on the coordinate system being used in geometry. The important thing to know is the Coordinate Reference Systems (CRS).





CRS
There are two main families of CRS. We have Geographic and Projected.



Geographic
Projected




These live on a sphere



Units: Degrees




Good for: Local mapping (example: State Plane - specific to USA).









Tip



For State Plane, it halves the state and draws a line of tangency through it before projecting it through a cylindrical projection. Then, this was passed through a coordinate grid system based on measured distance. Units: Feet OR meters. However, you need to check which unit of the State Plane you have is using.








Tip



The earth’s shape is a geoid (lumpy). However, this is inconvenient for measuring coordinates, so we approximate it to an ellipsoid with a flattening ratio. However, this is a poor fit (because it is an approximation). Thus, since the age of exploration, mathematicians and geographers have been attempting to minimize the errors in the fit.



Theoretical Steps to Creating a CRS

Flattening and approximating
Choosing a point to fix the ellipse to the earth’s surface (in the example of Clark 1866, this was Meades Ranch, KS. This created the North American Datum of 1927 - NAD27)







Tip



The NAD27 is not used anymore, though you may come across NAD83 which was calibrated via GRS-80 satellites instead. This is earth-centered.


Now, we commonly use WGS84. This is the GPS standard. However, while it is good for navigating, it is not good for geometric calculations. Hence, you generally do not want to use this in GIS. It also distorts the shapes, areas, distance, and direction when we do not project it.



Map Projections
All projections of the earth start with a 3D model of the earth that is subsequently flattened. Imagine you are holding a paper in the shape of a cylinder. With the earth model in the center, think about shining a light on the bottom and having the lines projected onto the cylinder. This is known as a cylindrical projection (one of the most well-known map projections uses this method: The Mercator projection). The closer the earth model is to the paper, the more accurate it is (no distortion). This is known as the line of tangency.

Transverse Cylindrical Projections
These use the cylinder on its side and projects via the longitude.


Conic Projections
These are more friendly to the countries in the higher latitudes as it is more accurate there.


Planar Projections
Usually best applied on island areas like Australia. They only have one point of tagency.

Setting and Changing the CRS in R

All data is going to come with a CRS. The most common problem you may face with this is that the CRS label is not attached to the data.

The code to attach it back is the St_set.crs(). If you want to change it to a different CRS, you should use St_transform().

Tip

5. Error Bars (Example)
county_data %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = NAME, y = estimate)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = estimate - moe, ymax = estimate + moe)) # errorbars have an upper and lower limit (how big you should make the error bars)
However, this plot has a lot of problems.

The names at the bottom are jumbled together
We have scientific notation (r defaults to this)
Default grid in the background
Data is out of order (so you can’t read anything)
Contrast is low
Too much data


Fixing the Plot
# let's make it less horrible
# reduce to 15 most unreliable.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>% # sort data from highest to lowest)
  slice_head(n = 15) %>% # now that it has been ordered, we are taking a slice from that head (15 of them). Then, this is being passed down to the ggplot
  ggplot(aes(x = NAME, y = estimate)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = estimate - moe, ymax = estimate + moe)) # this remains the same

## Flip to make names more readable:
county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = NAME, y = estimate)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = estimate - moe, ymax = estimate + moe)) +
  coord_flip() # flipping 

## Sort bars by bar length rather than alphabetically:
county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(NAME, estimate), y = estimate)) + # reorder the x column 
  geom_col() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = estimate - moe, ymax = estimate + moe)) +
  coord_flip()

## Remove "County, New York"

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  mutate(NAME = str_remove(NAME, " County, New York")) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(NAME, estimate), y = estimate)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = estimate - moe, ymax = estimate + moe)) +
  coord_flip()

#change to narrower width of the error bars

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  mutate(NAME = str_remove(NAME, " County, New York")) %>% # mutates the name column in the df to remove the specified string. Since you are specifying NAME, you are just modifying the df instead. As this is run within this plot, it doesn't change the actual df
  slice_head(n = 15) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(NAME, estimate), y = estimate)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = estimate - moe, ymax = estimate + moe), width = 0.3) +
  coord_flip()

# tidy up with a nice theme:
county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  mutate(NAME = str_remove(NAME, " County, New York")) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(NAME, estimate), y = estimate)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = estimate - moe, ymax = estimate + moe), width = 0.3) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal()

# fix labels and numbers:

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  mutate(NAME = str_remove(NAME, " County, New York")) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(NAME, estimate), y = estimate)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = estimate - moe, ymax = estimate + moe), width = 0.3) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(
    title = "Counties with the largest margins of error",
    subtitle = "People below 100% of the poverty level, ACS 2023 5-year estimates",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Population below poverty level"
  )



Coefficient of Variation (CV)

Relative measure of sampling error
\[\frac{\text{standard error}}{\text{estimate}} * 100\]




CV Threshold
Reliability




Low CV
15% -> High Reliability


Medium CV
15-30%


High CV
30% or more -> Low Reliability (High Sampling Error)





Derived Uncertainty
\[\text{poverty rate} = \frac{\text{number in poverty}\pm moe}{\text{total population} \pm moe}\]
moe_sum() # adding estimates together
moe_prop() # one estimate as a share of another
moe_ratio() # two completely different calculations. eg. ratio of people in poverty / household income. One is NOT a subset of the other


Looking back at the ACS

It measures change over time. Note the overlapping intervals. Eg. When you are asking it for 2023 data, it covers 2019-2023. When you are asking it for 2022 data, it covers 2018-2022.
If you are studying change over time, you want non-overlapping intervals. Eg. 2014-2018 and 2019 to 2023. However, you must note that their MOEs will likely be different


Working with an Example

Let’s say we have two ACS datasets

2014 - 2018: $45,000 with a MOE of 8,000
2019 - 2023: $62,000 with a MOE of 11,000

We need to get into the maths of the Standard Error of Difference

\[SE_{diff} = \sqrt{{SE_1}^2 + {SE_2}^2}\] \[Z = (\text{est}_1 - \text{est}_2)\]

In this case, when we fill in the numbers:

\[SE_{diff} = \sqrt{({\frac{8000}{1.645})}^2 + ({\frac{11000}{1.645})}^2}\]
